analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal, state-run national health program covering everyone, funded by new payroll and excise taxes.
analysis.headline: A bill to create universal government-run health coverage, with long-term care benefits, died in the Senate Finance Committee with only one cosponsor and never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made every U.S. citizen and lawful resident eligible for a comprehensive state-run health program covering doctor visits, hospital care, drugs, mental health care, and long-term care, funded mainly by the federal government with new payroll, income, corporate, and excise taxes. It would have repealed Medicare and Medicaid, limited private insurance to services the public program does not cover, and required doctors and hospitals to accept the program's payment as payment in full. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident would be eligible for comprehensive health coverage, including hospital care, physician services, prescription drugs, preventive care, mental health and substance-abuse treatment, and institutional and home-based long-term care, with enrollment decoupled from employment and automatic default coverage for anyone who does not sign up [S2] [S3]. Out-of-pocket costs would be tightly capped: a $100 individual ($300 family) deductible, $5 first-visit copay, copays capped at 20%, annual out-of-pocket limits of $1,000-$2,000 per family, and no cost-sharing at all for inpatient care or preventive services [S3]. Providers participating in the program would have to accept the state-set payment as payment in full, ending balance billing, and private insurance could only be sold for services the state program does not cover [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, insured and uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Makes every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident eligible for covered health and long-term care services in their state of residence, with automatic default enrollment for anyone who fails to sign up.

Covers a broad benefit package including hospital care, physician services, prescription drugs, preventive care, mental health and substance-abuse treatment, hospice, and both institutional and home-based long-term care with respite care for family caregivers.
Separates health coverage from employment, so changing or losing a job would no longer change or end coverage.
Caps out-of-pocket costs at $1,000-$2,000 per family per year, charges no cost-sharing for inpatient or preventive care, and requires affordable access rules for low-income people.
Bars participating providers from billing patients beyond the program's payment, ending balance bills and surprise charges for covered services.
Prohibits the sale of private insurance duplicating covered services, keeping everyone in one risk pool rather than letting healthier people buy their way out.
Directs federal money toward medically underserved and rural areas, including incentives to attract health professionals to them.

analysis.who_pays: Workers would pay a new 1% payroll tax with no wage cap, employers a 4% excise tax on wages above $30,000 (5% if the employer pays the employee's share), and the self-employed 5%, plus a 50% tax on what employers spend on retiree health coverage [S2] [S3]. The top individual income tax rate would rise from 31% to 33%, the corporate rate from 34% to 44%, 85% of Social Security benefits would become taxable instead of half, a new 2% tax would fall on unearned income, and cigarette and liquor taxes would more than triple [S2] [S3]. States would also have to fund their share from their own taxes [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill raises taxes on nearly everyone: a 1% employee payroll tax with no wage cap, a 4% employer tax on wages over $30,000, a 5% self-employment tax, a higher 33% top income tax rate, a 44% corporate rate, a 2% tax on unearned income, taxation of 85% of Social Security benefits, and sharply higher cigarette and liquor taxes.
It repeals Medicare and Medicaid outright, moving seniors, disabled people, and low-income Americans into newly created state programs whose approved plans and payment levels are untested.

A new National Health Care Commission would set national standards, budgets, and fee schedules, and could reduce federal payments to states that fall short of approval or place their entire program in federal receivership — a large transfer of control over health care from states and patients to a federal board.
The Commission may limit the duration or scope of covered services in order to allocate spending to optimize population health, an explicit cost-control lever that critics would read as rationing.
Long-term care would be gated by care-manager assessments, and respite care for family caregivers would be capped at 30 days or 720 hours a year.
Private insurance could no longer cover any service the state program covers, eliminating the option to buy faster or broader access to covered care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core offer is large: universal coverage including long-term care, capped out-of-pocket costs, and an end to job-linked coverage, paid for with broad, progressive-leaning taxes. But the bill is a heavy lift by design — it dismantles Medicare and Medicaid rather than building on them, concentrates enormous power in a federal commission that can cap services and seize control of state programs, and its revenue plan touches nearly every taxpayer and consumer. The trade-off — guaranteed care for everyone versus higher taxes, less private coverage, and government-managed limits on care — is real, and the bill's drafters chose the most sweeping version of it. Whether that bargain is good depends heavily on how well the new state programs and the Commission actually performed, which the bill leaves to implementation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never came up again, dying quietly when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kerrey introduced the bill on July 11, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a Senate Democrat, over its entire lifespan.
The bill would have repealed Medicare and Medicaid and limited private health insurance to services not covered by the new state programs.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, employers, and everyone financially invested in the existing employment-based, multi-payer system kept the status quo. The uninsured and underinsured people the bill named as its reason for being gained nothing from this attempt.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, employers, and the status quo

for.name: Sen. J. Robert Kerrey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 11, 1991; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, and no further action ever followed.

for.name: One Senate Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only senator besides Kerrey to do so.

against.name: Sen. Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: Received the referral; the committee never held a markup, hearing vote, or floor scheduling on the bill before the 102nd Congress ended.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed single-payer-style national health proposals that would restrict private coverage to supplemental services and concentrated their resources on defeating or marginalizing them during this period.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator, a Democrat, cosponsored the bill and no vote was ever held, so no party split appears anywhere in the record.

industries.note: Private insurance could be sold only for services the state program does not cover, which would eliminate the industry's core business of paying for hospital, physician, and drug care and replace it with a capped role selling supplemental policies.

The bill more than doubles the cigarette tax (from $12 or $25.20 to $30.50 or $64.05 per thousand) and raises the distilled spirits tax from $13.50 to $50 per proof gallon to fund the program; the taxes are designed to be paid by consumers through higher prices.

Employers would owe a new 4% excise tax on wages above $30,000 and a 50% tax on spending on retiree coverage, but the bill's stated goals include freeing employers from the administrative burden and cost of providing health coverage.

Providers would gain a universal payer and an end to uncompensated care for the uninsured, but would have to accept state-set fee schedules as payment in full and stay within expenditure targets, giving up balance billing and much pricing power.

Prescription drugs would become a covered benefit for everyone, expanding the customer base, but state payment schedules and Commission reviews of drug effectiveness would set the prices and could discontinue payment for products judged inefficient.
